questions.title: What would you actually look forward to?
questions.prompt: Drag the activities you would most enjoy into priority order. Rank just the ones that matter to you.

questions.title: What would make it rewarding for you, too?
questions.prompt: What would leave you feeling that advising was time well spent? Rank the possibilities that resonate with you, or add your own. No additional benefit needed is also an option.
questions.decision: Propose reciprocal benefits without inferring career ambitions or promising publicity.

options.label: See students grow in confidence and shape their own futures

questions.title: What most concerns you about students’ futures?
questions.prompt: Thinking about the next few years, which student challenges would you most like the club to address? Prioritize up to three, or rank more when it helps clarify your thinking.
questions.decision: Elicit concerns without treating them as verified forecasts.

options.label: Relying on AI without building understanding or judgment
Struggling to find entry-level opportunities or show their abilities

questions.title: How much would you like to help with your top three concerns?
questions.prompt: Set a level for each of your top three concerns. Tied concerns at the cutoff stay together.
questions.left: A small part of my contribution
questions.right: A main focus of my contribution
questions.decision: Desired focus for each leading concern, stored by concern ID. Not an allocation of hours or a measure of expertise.

questions.title: Students are building their first AI prototype. How would you help?

questions.decision: Preferred coaching mix for an inexperienced team, not an autonomy score.

questions.prompt: With your other commitments in mind, what range would be realistic in an ordinary week? Include routine meetings, messages, preparation, and project review. Discuss extra event preparation and special meetings separately.
questions.decision: Desired weekly range, not a measure of dedication. Zero and nonrecurring arrangements are valid.

context.title: What could a bite-sized AI Lab study look like?
paragraphs: One practical question, a small comparison, and a short write-up. Pair students with interested Dallas College IT staff or colleagues from other departments to investigate AI behavior together.
For example: Does an answer drift during a long conversation? Does a guardrail work consistently on harmless test cases? Does a generated explanation match the evidence?

The team could prepare an evidence brief for Dallas College senior leadership: what was tested, what was observed, the limitations, and what the findings suggest for a tool choice, pilot, guardrail, or staff-training decision. A small experiment informs a decision; it does not establish that a system is ready for deployment.

MATS connects research fellows with experienced mentors. Its research offers an example of learning through mentored investigation. This proposed Dallas College version would be smaller, student-centered, and focused on practical college questions—not a MATS program or affiliation.
Use approved tools and public or synthetic data. Staff participation, scope, permissions, and the audience for findings would be agreed with the people involved.

link.label: Explore MATS research — an example of mentored AI research
